items.title: Introducing new self-learning context enrichment in Knowledge Catalog
items.author: Vasiya KrishnanProduct Lead
items.content:
Today, we’re launching self-learning context enrichment (preview) and a reimagined Knowledge Studio experience (preview) in Knowledge Catalog, Google Cloud’s context engine for agents. Building on Knowledge Catalog's existing Gemini-powered enrichment, self-learning enrichment analyzes agent and user interactions to find gaps and keep your business context accurate and current. Knowledge Studio is the new command center for context engineers and data stewards to explore their data estate conversationally, navigate a visual context graph, and review proposed changes to the context graph before they are published to their users and agents.

An agent is only as good as the organization-wide definitions, rules, and relationships it reasons over — the context, as it were. That’s why curating context has become one of the most important disciplines in enterprise agentic capabilities. Today, most of that work happens by hand. Context engineers write prompts and mappings agent by agent, while data stewards try to manually keep definitions current across thousands of assets. But this breaks down as organizations move from a handful of agents to thousands, and eventually millions.

Knowledge Catalog’s Gemini-powered self-learning enrichment turns that manual upkeep into a continuous feedback loop. By analyzing agent and user interactions, it pinpoints missing or outdated context and pulls verified definitions from playbooks, code repositories, and business documents into governed, reusable context sets. Then, with optimized search, every agent gets precisely the right context it needs instead of reasoning over bloated prompts and raw schemas, and benefits from shared learning across your organization. Knowledge Catalog makes AI agents nearly 4X more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens, based on internal benchmarks.

Keep context current with Gemini-powered self-learning enrichment

Consider a simple question to a Gemini agent: "What was the net revenue in EMEA last quarter?" Answering it correctly requires knowing how your company defines net revenue, which tables hold the bookings, and how they join, yet that knowledge is typically scattered across a finance playbook in Google Docs, a data model in GitHub, and a Confluence page. Static catalogs expect subject matter experts to manually capture and update business definitions, metrics, and other context upfront so that an agent can effectively query the right data. However, in reality, experts rarely have the time to document every asset, and the moment the finance team revises how partner credits are treated next quarter, static definitions fall behind and every agent with a hardcoded formula starts giving the wrong answer.

Knowledge Catalog’s enrichment capability acts where you already keep your business knowledge: across your team’s every doc, repo, and table. It connects to your structured data across first-party and third-party sources and unstructured data in Cloud Storage, Google Workspace, GitHub, Confluence, and SharePoint. It finds, extracts, assembles, and maintains that business knowledge for you, linking those unstructured sources like playbooks and wikis and their context to your structured metadata in Knowledge Catalog like tables and schemas to make your structured data far more discoverable and actionable. On demand or on a schedule, it proposes business definitions, table and column descriptions, join relationships, golden queries, and task-specific agent instructions, each with source citations and a confidence score. On every run, it detects what changed at the source, retires obsolete definitions, and flags conflicts for review.

It learns from both your user and agent interactions. You can configure enrichment to analyze interaction traces from Gemini agents, Conversational Analytics in BigQuery, or your custom agents while redacting PII, and it pinpoints where agents struggled, such as ambiguous column lookups, ungrounded metrics, missing definitions, or users rephrasing the same question. It then finds the authoritative answer and stages a fix, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice. That's how context engineering keeps pace with millions of agent interactions, freeing experts to review changes instead of writing them from scratch.

Automation doesn't mean giving up control. You can choose to enable or disable auto-publishing at any time, and set the exact confidence score (for example, 85%) at which proposed changes are automatically approved. Anything below your threshold, along with sensitive updates such as deletions, become a Change Request for a steward to approve, edit, or reject. You can also provide your own evaluation set to test proposed updates end to end. Every change is logged with full provenance and can be reverted. And of course, Google never uses your data to train its models.

Set the right context for each audience with context sets

By design, an enterprise context graph is quite broad, but for a given task, both agents and users often only need the right, trusted segment of it. Knowledge Catalog achieves that with context sets — curated, governed subsets of the context graph that contains the definitions, metrics, join logic, and golden queries for a specific domain, team, agent, or group of end users. For instance, a sales agent can be bound to the Sales context set, while a finance analyst's assistant can be bound to the Finance context set. Because "net revenue" can legitimately mean different things to each group, every domain maintains its own definitions in the same catalog. However, agents don't have to be bound to a single set; with search in Knowledge Catalog, an agent can also dynamically search and find the right context set for any given task.

Context sets also provide built-in data governance and fine-grained access control. Access to each context set is managed with IAM, so stewards decide which agents and users can read, use, or edit it. Agents only retrieve context from the sets they're authorized to use, and access to the underlying data continues to follow your existing permissions. Every update is traceable, and reversible, and because context sets build on the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), you can import an OKF bundle to become a context set and export it back out as OKF so your context stays portable.

Explore and govern it all in Knowledge Studio

All of these capabilities come together in the reimagined Knowledge Catalog experience, built for context engineers and data stewards who curate and govern context for agents.

The new Knowledge Studio turns Knowledge Catalog from a repository of static inventory into an interactive command center, allowing you to:

  • See context coverage at a glance: Navigate a visual map of your cross-cloud data estate, from operational databases and warehouses to semantic models, context sets, and documentation.
  • Explore context conversationally: Ask business questions in natural language, traverse relationships across your enterprise context graph, and see exactly how agents reason over your metadata.
  • Review and validate enrichments in one place: Inspect each proposed change, source citations, and confidence score. Test context sets against real questions, and approve, edit, or roll back change requests with software-style version control.
  • Track each enrichment task's schedule, results, token usage, and run duration, and get notified by email when a run completes.

These features will be rolled out to customers in the next few weeks. Sign up to request immediate access and visit the documentation for step-by-step guidance.

items.title: Introducing Agent Compute Engine and expanded agent governance
items.author: The Google Cloud infrastructure team
items.content:
Nirav Mehta, VP Product Management; Michael Bachman, VP/GM; Kevin Hutchins, VP Product Management

Scaling Gemini to planet scale taught us firsthand that securely running autonomous agents is fundamentally an infrastructure challenge. The shift from single-turn prompting to interactive agents requires a new paradigm of execution and control. To support massive concurrent agent sessions, we engineered new compute and governance solutions for Gemini to help solve these challenges.

Today at AGNTCon + MCPCon, we are delivering these capabilities to customers by launching , a purpose-built compute service that already powers Gemini as an agent for work tasks. It will be available in preview in the coming months, providing hardware-isolated runtime sandbox security. Additionally, we are extending Gemini for business’ agent governance capabilities to support agents wherever they operate. Together, these capabilities deliver the control you need to run, govern, and scale your agents.

Under the hood of Agent Compute Engine

Agent Compute Engine arose from the need to handle Google’s massive agentic workloads that write and execute code, run tools, drive browsers, orchestrate enterprise workflows, and iterate rapidly and at scale. While traditional compute primitives are excellent for standard workloads, they weren't optimized for the unique, highly iterative nature of AI agents.

Purpose-built for agents, Agent Compute Engine gives every Gemini agent its own high-performance, secure computer to act upon, powering Gemini's dynamic, high-churn sessions. Agent Compute Engine is optimized specifically for the unique lifecycle patterns of AI agents, and you will soon be able to use this service to power your own custom agents. Highlights include:

  • Agents start, pause, and resume constantly and require an architecture that delivers speed, at scale, all with extreme efficiency. Agent Compute Engine delivers microVMs that boot rapidly, so an agent loop or an eval sweep doesn’t wait on infrastructure. Further, supporting Google users with multiple agents requires a cost-effective solution that can get the most out of a physical machine. Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore. When an agent finishes executing a tool call and enters the “thinking” phase of the agentic loop, the microVM signals that it's idle, and the host moves it from an active to an idle state. In other words, it can pause a running microVM while an agent waits on a human or an external system, and quickly resume it from snapshots.
  • Enhanced security, isolation and governance: As agents take on more complex tasks, the risk of untrusted or adversarial code executing inside a sandbox is an ever-present reality. By running Agent Compute Engine with Titanium, Google’s offload infrastructure processing unit (IPU), we deliver silicon-rooted defense-in-depth built for untrusted AI agents Agent Compute Engine delivers strong isolation via a hardware-isolated Cloud Hypervisor boundary with its own guest kernel and root access. (For a closer look at Agent Compute Engine’s microVM architecture and security, read the technical deep dive.) Each microVM runs its agent’s own identity, using short-lived credentials. Every microVM also gets its own cryptographically verified ID, and service credentials are injected in egress outside the microVM. Integrated with Agent Gateway, Agent Compute Engine delivers comprehensive observability, policy and security evaluation.
  • Persistence and enterprise integration: Agents require the ability to persist agent data across multiple, long-running sessions. To solve this, each Agent Compute Engine microVM has its own Hyperdisk, enabling persistence of execution workspaces and agent context. In addition, in order to do meaningful work, they need the ability to use enterprise data without moving it. By weaving Agent Compute Engine directly into Google’s cloud and identity fabric, enterprise connectivity is governed by the exact same security and identity model that protects the microVM itself, enabling a unified identity model as well as auditability.

Gautham Thambidorai, VP & Google Fellow, Gemini

Building on GKE with Agent Substrate

For platform teams looking for customization and multi-cloud portability, or who have already standardized on Kubernetes, Agent Substrate on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is an open-source execution runtime that brings the same agent-first design to Kubernetes. It’s built on a zero-trust architecture that cleanly decouples agent execution from machine management. When an agent becomes idle, Agent Substrate snapshots its active memory and returns the machine to the pool, then resumes the agent the moment it’s needed again. Because it’s open source and Kubernetes-native, you can customize it, extend it, and run it alongside your existing workloads. Some Agent Substrate highlights include:

  • Agent Substrate delivers as much as 10x higher compute density compared to traditional compute while maintaining full kernel isolation and identity-based network security for every agent.
  • In benchmark validation running 200,000 agents, Agent Substrate sustained 500 activations per second at less than 500 ms suspend and resume latency.
  • Think of Agent Substrate as zero-trust for agents. Each sandbox has strong hardware isolation built in using your choice of microVM or gVisor and every agent gets its own cryptographically secure identity paired with egress proxies that enforce granular network policies and inject credentials outside the reach of the agents themselves. Looking ahead, we will expand the Agent Substrate runtime architecture to integrate with our broader Gemini for business governance framework.
  • Runs on any Kubernetes cluster in any compute environment and works with any agent framework or harness, including Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes.
  • : Integrates with Filestore agent volumes with sub-second resume latency to scale alongside active compute, providing a single shared workspace for multi-agent workflows.

Expanding governance capabilities for agents everywhere

As organizations transition autonomous agents from isolated pilots to multi-runtime production fleets, traditional security frameworks must be hardened and evolve. Customers face a triple challenge: securing dynamic non-deterministic interaction paths across agents, tools, models, skills and data; maintaining a default deny posture with least-privilege-access distributed runtimes; and ensuring that asynchronous agent actions can be audited. Without strong agent governance, agent sprawl quickly introduces risk — including shadow AI, data exfiltration, and agent actions that are hard to track and audit.

To solve these challenges, we built robust agent governance capabilities into Gemini platform, including:

  • Serves as the air traffic controller for client-to-agent and agents-to-anywhere traffic. It integrates a broad set of governance and security policies including sensitive data protection, agent attack protection, semantic governance, and the ability to bring your own policy.
  • Provides a central repository that serves as the source of truth for all approved running agents, tools, MCP servers, skills, models and endpoints, governing runtime access via applied policies.
  • Assigns a unique secure ID using open standard based SPIFFE to each agent, acting as the digital signature for authentication, access control, and auditing.
  • Provides OpenTelemetry (OTel)-compliant telemetry adopting agentic semantic conventions, emitting standardized metrics, logs, and distributed traces for every model call, tool invocation, and agent hop across Agent Gateway.

Now as agent fleets continue to grow dramatically across diverse environments, we are extending the reach of our Gemini for business agent governance capabilities across Google Cloud runtimes, cross-cloud, on-prem and client devices to manage and secure agents everywhere they run. This includes the following capabilities:

  • Broad Google Cloud runtime coverage Extends comprehensive agent governance across Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, Agent Sandboxes in Gemini platform, GKE, and Agent Compute Engine (preview).
  • Consistent cross-cloud reach: Deploys lightweight, Envoy proxy-based policy enforcement points to extend governance to multicloud and hybrid environments (in preview soon).
  • Governance for local agents on endpoints Extends governance to coding agents like Claude Code and Antigravity CLI on managed devices with an OS-level sandbox and local governance services (in preview soon).

Additionally we are announcing new agent governance capabilities to to enable granular cost controls, intelligent model routing, and simplified customizations and integrations. Highlights coming this quarter in preview include:

  • Granular token and cost governance:Token management provides control over token consumption across agents and models, allowing you to attribute spend, enforce budget guardrails, and provide a single source of truth for token metrics.
  • Route requests to the right model: Model routing policies route user and agent requests to the right model, controlling costs and improving performance.
  • Service Extensions bindings add streamlined support for inline programmability and extensibility. Allows tightly integrating Google services, customers’ bespoke functions, and partner services directly into the datapath.
  • Simplified and secure agent-to-tool connectivity: Express Link for Cloud Run allows agents to declare what they need to reach, and it establishes the secure, authenticated connection between components, including identity token injection.

Build on our resilient agent infrastructure

The agentic era requires an evolution in how we scale infrastructure. By combining the high-performance execution of Agent Compute Engine and Agent Substrate with agent governance capabilities from Gemini for business — now expanded with cross-cloud reach — we are establishing a resilient foundation for protected, high-density AI agents.

items.title: ZenteiQ scales batch inference 4x with GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d
items.author: Fisayo FeyisetanProduct Manager, Google Kubernetes Engine
items.content:
, an artificial intelligence startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and selected under the to build sovereign scientific foundation models from the ground up. To pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators. - Fisayo Feyisetan, Product Manager, Google Cloud

Unlike general-purpose language models trained primarily on web text and code, scientific foundation models must understand complex physical systems, mathematical governing equations, and numerical solvers across domains such as thermodynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and electromagnetics. At ZenteiQ, we are building sovereign scientific foundation models from scratch that interpret simulation outputs, evaluate equation formulations, and work through step-by-step mathematical derivations that obey physical laws.

Pre-training models on large datasets of governing equations takes hundreds of billions of reasoning tokens. Alongside curated scientific literature and simulation datasets, we also rely on a batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that we independently designed and implemented to generate, evaluate, and filter candidate derivations and solver validation problems before feeding them into our MaxText pre-training jobs.

Because we operate on a fixed compute allocation, every hour our accelerators spend generating and verifying training data is an hour taken away from pre-training. When data generation falls behind, multi-host accelerator clusters reserved for pre-training sit idle, waiting on datasets.

When data generation slows down pre-training

To maximize data generation speed, our pipeline separates prompt preparation on worker pods from model serving on vLLM across multi-node accelerator pools. Each batch moves through four stages: expanding scientific seed concepts into prompt batches, generating candidate reasoning traces with generator models, scoring responses using evaluator models, and running guardrail checks with a separate model family before packaging verified datasets for pre-training.

We originally ran these model pools on Kubernetes with standard ClusterIP round-robin load balancing across inference endpoints. As we scaled our pipeline to feed our 9B- and 35B-parameter model schedules, two routing bottlenecks began slowing down dataset creation.

  • Our upstream worker pods expand seed concepts into prompts of widely varying complexity and response length. Because standard round-robin load balancing had no visibility into vLLM engine queues, it kept sending new requests to serving pods that were already busy processing long reasoning traces, while neighboring nodes had capacity to spare.
  • Redundant prefix computation: Prompts within a generation batch share roughly 70% to 80% of their instructional context and task specifications. Round-robin routing scattered requests with identical instructions across different serving instances, forcing each pod to recompute the same shared prompt prefix from scratch instead of reusing warm caches in accelerator memory.

Together, uneven queues and redundant prefill work caused our generation throughput to swing by as much as half within a single run, stretching out dataset creation and delaying the start of scheduled pre-training runs. We needed routing that understood live vLLM queue depths and prompt caches, without pulling our researchers off model development to build and maintain a custom inference scheduler.

Building on GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d

We already run our data preparation and MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE, which lets our team manage data generation and model training on the same Kubernetes platform. Following a recommendation from Google Cloud to address our routing bottlenecks without changing our underlying scientific methodology or pipeline design, we deployed GKE Inference Gateway, powered by the open-source llm-d distributed inference framework, in front of our vLLM accelerator pools.

In our pipeline, worker pods pull scientific seed documents and domain taxonomies from Cloud Storage and expand them into batches of multi-step prompts. Those batches flow through a single GKE Inference Gateway deployment that manages traffic across all of our model families and serving nodes.

Rather than maintaining isolated routing for each model tier, we route generation requests, evaluation queries, and guardrail checks across their respective model pools through the same gateway. Once candidate responses pass evaluation and guardrail checks, worker pods deduplicate and package the verified datasets for direct consumption by downstream MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE.

From round-robin to load- and cache-aware routing

With GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d, routing decisions use live serving signals from our vLLM instances rather than static round-robin rotation. GKE Inference Gateway continuously monitors real-time queue depth and key-value (KV) cache utilization across our vLLM endpoints. When a serving node is busy decoding a long equation derivation, the gateway routes incoming requests to nodes with open capacity, so heavy prompts no longer pile up behind busy workers while neighboring nodes sit idle.

At the same time, the gateway routes requests with matching scientific instructions to the serving node where that prefix’s KV cache is already warm in accelerator memory. Because 70% to 80% of each prompt is shared instructional context while the generated reasoning trajectories vary from request to request, combining prefix-cache locality with live queue balancing lets our pods skip repeated prefill work without overloading any single replica.

Higher throughput, predictable training runs

Adopting GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d transformed the speed and predictability of our data generation pipeline. Across our production clusters, intelligent routing delivered:

  • 4x higher fleet throughput: Aggregate throughput jumped from 16,964 to 69,114 tokens per second per 1,000 accelerators — growing daily output from 1.47 billion to nearly 6 billion generated tokens.
  • 3.5x to 5.5x gains across individual model pools: Real-time queue balancing kept serving nodes evenly loaded throughout each run, preventing the mid-run slowdowns caused by long reasoning derivations.
  • 14-percentage-point higher prefix-cache hit rate: Routing prompts with matching scientific instructions to warm caches avoided redundant prefill work before each request branched into its own derivation.

For our research and infrastructure teams, the most important outcome was schedule predictability. Quadrupling daily output meant verified datasets were ready on time, so our multi-host pre-training runs started on schedule instead of waiting on data generation.

What’s next for physical AI at ZenteiQ

As we scale our scientific foundation models from 9B to 35B parameters and beyond, we plan to use the same GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d routing setup for post-training reinforcement learning (RL) and automated numerical solver evaluation loops. Because each turn in those multi-turn rollouts builds on the context of the turns before it, they depend even more heavily on live queue balancing and warm prefix caches.

items.title: BigQuery ObjectRef now GA: Build multimodal data platforms for conversational analytics entirely in SQL
items.author: Jamy SuProduct Manager
items.content:
For data science, data engineering, and machine learning teams, unlocking the value of unstructured data, such as images, videos, audio, and documents, has historically meant managing siloed data pipelines for structured and unstructured data, and for analytics and AI/ML use cases. Even when files remain in Cloud Storage, running inference requires teams to orchestrate external machine learning workloads, only to face the complex, brittle challenge of stitching those structured inference outputs back into the data warehouse for analysis. This post-hoc data-stitching introduces significant operational overhead and database misalignment.

and multimodal data analytics in BigQuery are now in General Availability (GA), establishing BigQuery as a comprehensive, multimodal agentic data platform.

With ObjectRef, BigQuery natively bridges the gap between Cloud Storage and your analytical engine. You can represent unstructured data as native ObjectRef columns directly alongside your traditional relational columns. This unlocks a massive advantage over standalone model APIs by enabling you to pass multimodal, multi-column inputs directly to Gemini models in a single SQL query or natural language query using conversational analytics. ObjectRef integrations with BigQuery AI, conversational analytics in BigQuery and Gemini Enterprise enable you to easily combine Cloud Storage files with rich, structured database context, metadata, timestamps and custom agent instructions.

You can now leverage BigQuery's core strengths (fully serverless compute, low total cost of ownership, and built-in at-scale inference) to build, run, and govern powerful unstructured-to-structured, unstructured-to-unstructured and fully multimodal-to-multimodal pipelines without separate compute clusters. Crucially, the extracted features and annotations can be combined directly with the unstructured object itself by storing the ObjectRef in the same row. Using this combined data directly in conversational analytics and AI agents avoids the loss of nuanced data and context that typically occurs when customers transform unstructured files into purely structured formats. Customers are already using this approach to generate embeddings for multimodal vector search, perform at-scale classification using GenAI, and execute precise data and feature extraction from vast archives of documents and media, all via standard SQL.

ObjectRef brings structure to the unstructured

ObjectRef is a built-in, predefined STRUCT data type that points to objects outside of BigQuery.

By storing these pointers natively in standard BigQuery tables alongside traditional columns, BigQuery treats unstructured files as first-class data citizens. Furthermore, this architecture supports independent data lifecycles: your GCS data and BigQuery tables can change independently without affecting the underlying data in the other system.

This approach serves multiple data personas by offering powerful advantages:

  • Keep your high-volume media files securely in Cloud Storage and query them instantly in BigQuery, respecting data gravity and avoiding costly data duplication.
  • SQL and Python interoperability: You can query unstructured data using standard SQL or BigQuery DataFrames. Crucially, you can pass ObjectRefs into BigQuery Python UDFs, allowing you to bring open-source Python libraries, like OpenCV, directly to your data to execute custom logic without moving it.
  • Independent lifecycles and versioning: ObjectRefs ensure reproducible inference by tracking specific GCS generation numbers. If the underlying GCS file changes, your query can still reference the exact version of the file that existed when the row was written.
  • You can secure, audit, and share access to both structured columns and their related unstructured files using BigQuery's existing security policies and IAM controls.

Create full-fidelity ETL with SQL

Since launching ObjectRef in preview, a powerful, highly effective pattern has emerged among our users: building full-fidelity ETL pipelines entirely with SQL.

Teams are leveraging BigQuery’s serverless architecture to integrate AI/ML directly into their data environments, eliminating the need for separate compute clusters to handle data movement and inference. Managing unstructured data in GCS as standard BigQuery columns allows users to apply core data engineering best practices, such as building idempotent pipelines, ensuring reproducibility, and executing seamless backfills, directly to images, video, audio, and documents.

Once data is robustly prepared, teams use Gemini within BigQuery to execute full-fidelity ETL. They unlock by extracting features and annotating unstructured data while keeping the original ObjectRef anchored in the same row. The structured outputs power fast filtering, reporting and BI dashboards, while the attached unstructured objects remain available for deep, context-heavy reasoning. For example, you might extract sentiment scores and topic tags from an archive of customer call recordings to quickly flag at-risk accounts on a BI dashboard (the structured layer). Simultaneously, a conversational analytics agent evaluating escalation processes can seamlessly fall back to the original audio files to analyze the caller and customer service representative interactions, preventing the loss of critical nuance that typically occurs in unstructured-to-structured ETL pipelines.

items.title: Managed RAG search inside the sovereign perimeter: Gemini on GDC enterprise search
items.author: Rohan GroverSenior Director, Google Distributed Cloud
items.content:
National security agencies and other sovereign and highly regulated organizations handle incredibly sensitive data such as classified reports, field manuals, and sensitive multi-modal datasets. Search and multimodal intelligence that’s available in the public cloud can help teams manage and analyze that data, but due to strict data sovereignty mandates, that data cannot leave the customer premises.

The alternative has been to deploy custom agentic search inside a secure, disconnected perimeter, but until now, that meant months building and maintaining custom infrastructure — stitching together models, building speech-to-text and optical character recognition (OCR) pipelines, configuring vector databases, and managing a bespoke user interface.

Today, we're excited to announce enterprise search capabilities with Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped accelerated by NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to help solve the above challenges. In preview, this fully managed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) search experience runs entirely inside your physical security perimeter, with no connection to the public internet or to Google Cloud's global infrastructure. Your teams can now upload their files into a conversation and ask Gemini to find information about it, summarize it, compare it, or translate it. Every answer cites its sources, and conversations persist between sessions.

Enterprise search capabilities on GDC enable your teams to search across siloed data and unlock powerful insights. With these capabilities, you can now:

  • Go from hundreds of pages to a cited answer: Ask questions across long manuals, reports, and policies, and see exactly which files each answer came from.
  • Ask in one language and get answers grounded in documents written in another, or have Gemini translate them.
  • Ask one question across many formats: Combine audio recordings, video clips, images, and spreadsheets with no separate transcription or OCR steps.
  • Pick up where you left off: Conversations and files persist between sessions, so you don’t have to start from scratch on long-running work.
  • Keep access need-to-know: Each user's chats and files are private to that user, and access follows the identity provider groups you already manage.

Users can work with PDF, Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, plus TXT, HTML, PNG and JPEG images, WAV audio, and MP4 video. Each file can be up to 100 MB, and each chat up to 500 MB.

Core architectural layers: under the hood

Let's follow a user query through each layer of the stack: signing in, ingesting files, generating the response with Gemini, and storing the session. Every step happens on the organization's air-gapped network.

Users sign in through their organization's identity provider. Administrators map the service's user role to identity provider groups, and only members of those groups can access the application. Each user's chats and uploaded files are private to that user.

Document ingestion and embedding

When a user uploads a file, it goes straight to the app's object storage bucket. The backend records the file's metadata in the app's managed PostgreSQL database, which is optimized for search. The backend then splits the file into chunks, such as groups of PDF pages or tiles of an image, and writes them to the bucket. A Gemini embedding model running natively within the GDC deployment converts each chunk into a vector, which the backend stores in the app's PostgreSQL database.

When the user asks a question, the state-of-the-art (SOTA) Gemini model running entirely on GDC inside the customer’s data center first rewrites the question with context from the conversation. The backend then embeds the rewritten question with the same model and searches the vector database.

The backend then combines the question, the conversation history, and the best-matching data into a single multimodal prompt and sends it to a Gemini endpoint running on NVIDIA HGX B300 systems in that same GDC deployment. Gemini is natively multimodal — it accepts text, images, audio, and video as input, so it can reason across data coming from different file types in a single context, and doesn't require separate speech-to-text and OCR models. The answer then streams back to the user with citations to the source files.

Lastly, the persistence layer keeps each conversation's state. Each question and answer is stored in the system’s database and uploaded files stay in object storage, so users can reopen an earlier session and pick up where they left off.

Built for classified and sovereign environments

With Gemini and enterprise search on GDC, prompts, responses, uploaded documents, and embeddings never leave your organization's air-gapped network, and every model runs locally. Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 disk encryption using locally managed HSM keys, and in transit with TLS using FIPS-approved algorithms. Local IAM integration with granular role-based access control (RBAC) governs access to resources. GDC air-gapped has U.S. DoD IL6 accreditation and is designed to support strict requirements in alignment with FedRAMP High security controls.

Code execution: Compliance and security

To deliver precise, deterministic answers from structured spreadsheet data (such as CSV and XLSX files), Gemini enterprise search leverages the Gemini inference stack's local code-execution engine.

When handling analytical queries — such as computing the average salary across departments — Gemini dynamically generates Python code and runs it securely within Agent Substrate, an open-source execution runtime built for large-scale agent orchestration.

To mitigate security risks inherent to executing LLM-generated code, Agent Substrate enforces strict network isolation and runs workloads inside gVisor sandboxes, helping ensure strong isolation boundaries without sacrificing inference performance.

Bringing frontier models to the sovereign data center

You no longer have to choose between uncompromising security and cutting-edge multimodal intelligence. Enterprise search, Gemini 3.5 Flash and databases optimized for search run together inside the GDC air-gapped perimeter with no dependency on the internet to bring the best autonomous capabilities to the sovereign cloud.

Explore the GDC air-gapped documentation and contact your GDC representative to learn how you can best leverage these search capabilities in your sovereign cloud.

items.title: Announcing llm-d 1.0: Open distributed inference for agents on Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs
items.author: Sean HorganProduct Manager
items.content:
Today at the PyTorch Conference, we released llm-d 1.0, an open-source, Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Co-founded by Google with Red Hat, IBM and others, we worked with a community of more than 500 contributors over 25 organizations on this Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, bringing together two important communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production.

llm-d 1.0 arrives at a time when agents are changing the nature of inference. A year ago, most inference traffic was chat: one prompt in, one response out. Today, workloads are shifting to multi-step agents and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts that fan out across tools, share long prefixes, and arrive in bursts. Serving them on a single machine — or behind a generic round-robin load balancer — breaks down fast. Replicas recompute the same prompts, accelerator memory fills up with duplicate state, and one bursty agent loop can stall interactive users.

llm-d solves this for teams serving their own models by turning a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool. During the PyTorch Conference keynote, we showed this in action with 1,000 sandboxed agents on Agent Substrate on GKE hitting a single llm-d endpoint across vLLM, SGLang, and a mixed fleet of Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. As traffic scaled across the three stages below, cache-aware routing and tiered KV cache kept each agent's steps on the replicas holding its context, while flow control queued bursty agent loops so interactive requests stayed fast.

llm-d already delivered prefix- and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference across Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. These capabilities provide:

  • Multi-tenant quality of service. Priority and fairness-aware routing via llm-d flow control, helping latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads share a fleet to meet SLOs without starving one another.
  • v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
  • Router high availability and zero-downtime updates, alongside DisaggregatedSet, which orchestrates prefill/decode-aware rolling updates without dropping context or disrupting active sessions.
  • Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, and native Responses API state, helping agents reuse context across turns.
  • . Native PyTorch model serving with TorchTPU co-operative time-slicing to raise throughput and utilization across Google Cloud TPU fleets.

The components are designed so that you can compose them into your own bespoke production environment. Keep your engine, model and cluster, and adopt only the serving components and configurations you need.

Across the areas below, Google engineers worked with the llm-d community to connect upstream Kubernetes primitives, PyTorch serving engines, and accelerator-aware scheduling into a composable stack.

One endpoint, many accelerators

An agent fleet is not one workload. Interactive turns need low latency, background loops and reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts need high throughput, and demand swings by the minute. llm-d puts your accelerator pools behind a single endpoint, with one router, one KV cache index, and one flow-control policy in front of the whole fleet. Agents call a single API; the router picks the replica for each step and keeps a session's context on the replicas that already hold it. Adding capacity, mixing accelerator generations, or moving a model to a different pool becomes a platform change, not an agent rewrite. TorchTPU brings Google Cloud TPUs into that fleet, running PyTorch models natively inside upstream vLLM and SGLang without model rewrites. For more, see the llm-d on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) TPU guide.

Routing that remembers context

The llm-d router builds on Gateway API Inference, the Kubernetes project for inference-optimized routing that we launched. On GKE, GKE Inference Gateway runs the llm-d router as a managed service, simplifying installation and management and extending routing across regions. The router tracks the replicas holding each cached prefix and weighs load and predicted latency when it picks one. When accelerator memory fills up, rather than dropping it, llm-d uses vLLM’s OffloadingConnector, Mooncake, or SGLang’s HiCache to move KV cache to host memory and then to SSD or Google Cloud Managed Lustre. This setup helps prevent prefix-eviction storms under heavy, multi-turn, and long-context conversational loads across mixed TPU and GPU fleets.

On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing plus host memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and raised total throughput 2.4x versus a plain Kubernetes Service, as of October 2026 (source).

Disaggregation that upgrades safely

Prefill is compute-heavy and decode is memory-bound, so running both on the same replicas makes each wait on the other. llm-d runs prefill, decode, and multimodal encode as separate pools, with wide expert parallelism spreading large mixture-of-experts models across nodes. In 1.0, DisaggregatedSet — built on LeaderWorkerSet, the Kubernetes API for multi-host inference that we started — manages these pools as one unit. Rolling updates move prefill and decode together on matching versions while each phase scales independently. For more, see the disaggregated serving guide.

Async inference that runs alongside real-time inference

For latency-tolerant traffic, llm-d 1.0 introduces llm-d-async-processor, which pulls requests from queues like Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis and routes them alongside real-time traffic. Using queue and pool-dispatch gates, the processor checks available capacity and enforces strict priority lanes and quotas so background jobs run in slack capacity without starving interactive users.

Time-slicing to put idle RL capacity to work

During RL training, accelerators often sit idle 40% to 60% of the time during rollout generation or weight updates. llm-d now supports Google Cloud TPU and GPU time-slicing to interleave async inference into those quiet cycles, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline to >70% (source).

Tuning a distributed inference stack across routers, KV cache tiers, and prefill/decode pools takes repeatable measurement under realistic multi-turn load. Prism is llm-d’s open-source analysis dashboard for exploring published benchmarks across llm-d’s well-lit paths, backed by standardized llm-d-benchmark recipes and inference-perf workloads. Inspect the exact configurations behind the numbers, or upload runs from your own cluster to compare throughput, latency, and cost curves side by side.

Running llm-d 1.0 on Google Cloud

llm-d builds on Kubernetes components you may already run: Gateway API, LeaderWorkerSet, Dynamic Resource Allocation, Prometheus, and OpenTelemetry. Running llm-d on Google Cloud brings these pieces together with managed infrastructure:

  • is the llm-d router operating in Gateway Mode, a managed GKE Gateway that handles the L7 proxy and load balancing and calls the llm-d Endpoint Picker on every request, simplifying installation and management so you don't run the proxy yourself. More importantly, GKE Inference Gateway is how you scale llm-d across clusters and regions with global failover and Model Armor safety checks.
  • Autoscaling on inference signals. KEDA and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scale pools based on queue depth, saturation, and predicted latency, while Kueue enforces per-model quota on shared accelerators.
  • Mixed accelerator node pools. Google Cloud TPU and GPU pools run behind the same llm-d endpoint, deployed with verified Helm charts.
  • KV cache offloading across layers. Google Cloud Managed Lustre provides a shared remote tier beneath local TPU and GPU HBM and host CPU RAM so long-context workloads run without exhausting accelerator memory.

This GKE llm-d stack carries production traffic, and it has been tested at fleet scale:

  • Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) serves production traffic through GKE Inference Gateway, doubling its prefix cache hit rate from 35% to 70%, cutting TTFT by more than 35% for coding agents and cutting P95 TTFT by more than 50% under bursty chat traffic (source).
  • In a published benchmark across a 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment serving a mixture-of-experts model in the US and Europe, multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway and the llm-d router scaled throughput 2.9x across three clusters with a 99.9% success rate and less than 1% routing overhead (source).
  • In a published benchmark on A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B-parameter model, llm-d with multi-connector KV cache offloading to Google Cloud Managed Lustre in addition to Host CPU RAM, delivered an approximately 40% improvement in TTFT and a 30% reduction in end-to-end latency responding to 50k-token prompts compared to CPU RAM offload only, while reducing GPU-hour requirements by nearly 60% (source).

Organizations running llm-d on Google Cloud are putting these same capabilities to work in different ways, for instance prefix-aware routing to raise cache hit rates, open interfaces that fit an existing service mesh, and flow control to hold latency for priority tiers when traffic spikes.

enforce strict priority bands across our commercial tiers paid traffic meets our latency SLOsMathis Felardos, Lucas Fernandes-Martins and Nikhil Thomas,

Teams serving their own models have been asking for an open stack they can take apart and adapt to their own infrastructure, with the cache-aware routing, traffic control, and upgrade controls required in production. llm-d 1.0 gives them that and a community to build with.

  1. Check out the full demo of llm-d with TPUs at the Google Cloud booth during the PyTorch Conference.

items.author: Bill JiaVice President, Engineering
items.content:
Today at PyTorch Conference 2026, we announced a range of new products and integrations designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure. Notably, TorchTPU, our native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, is now available as open source on GitHub. With TorchTPU, TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. You can now train, serve, and deploy models on TPUs using the tools you already rely on, including vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray, TorchRec, Hugging Face, LiteRT. Ultimately, this provides our customers choice across a broad range of workload-optimized computing options including TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs, with a consistent, open software and operational model across the full portfolio.

Run PyTorch code natively on TPUs

Co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU lets you run existing PyTorch workloads on TPUs with minimal code changes, using the familiar APIs. TorchTPU lets you debug your models with eager mode, then transition to production-level performance via torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. By supporting standard PyTorch APIs, advanced diagnostics, and native distributed primitives out of the box, TorchTPU unlocks high performance and operational efficiency from day one.

We also partnered with Hugging Face so that popular open-weight models across the Hugging Face Hub run natively on TorchTPU. In Transformers v5, deploying models to TPUs is now as simple as passing . The Diffusers library runs natively on TPUs with support for eager mode, torch.compile, and tensor parallelism to scale large generative models across multiple accelerators. To maintain consistent reliability, we also built dedicated CI/CD pipelines for continuous nightly testing of the Hugging Face Transformers suite on TPU infrastructure.

As reasoning and agentic models scale, inference cost and latency become the primary bottlenecks in production. We’ve integrated TorchTPU into widely used open-source serving engines and paired them with Kubernetes-native fleet routing across TPUs and GPUs to help you optimize throughput per dollar.

This foundation allows developers to scale workloads across diverse hardware while minimizing the friction of platform-specific tuning. To bring these framework-level enhancements to life in production, we have collaborated with leading open-source communities and industry partners. In the sections below, we explore how these partnerships are driving breakthrough efficiency across high-throughput serving with vLLM, structured agentic execution with SGLang, and large-scale distributed fleet orchestration with llm-d.

Deployment flexibility and operational efficiency

Get started with PyTorch on Google Cloud

Together, these releases reinforce our commitment to making the Google TPU software ecosystem an open, developer-friendly environment for the PyTorch community. By bringing native TPU support upstream into the PyTorch stack across TorchTPU, Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, VeRL, and Ray — and contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch Ecosystem — we are giving you the flexibility to build, adapt, and scale AI on your terms.

items.title: Introducing Gemini for government services
items.author: Thomas KurianCEO, Google Cloud
items.content:
Earlier this month at Gemini at Work, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent for work. It answers your questions, handles your knowledge work, creates your images and media, and writes and runs code. You give it objectives, not instructions, and come back to finished work. It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and has the security, administration, and governance your organization requires.

Every industry runs on knowledge a general model does not have. Government work runs on statute, regulation, and agency guidance, across siloed legacy systems, under strict requirements for data sovereignty, compliance, and confidentiality. Too often that leaves civil servants on data entry and manual document review instead of the services citizens depend on.

Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all.

Five components of Gemini for government services

Developed alongside agency leaders, Gemini for government services provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies with five core components:

  1. Skills for government work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Each one applies the statute, regulation, and agency guidance that govern that task, so an agency's standard operating procedures carry into the work Gemini supports.
  2. Connectors to agency systems: Secure connectors link Gemini to the case management, ERP, HR, and collaboration systems agencies already run, along with authoritative federal data sources. Gemini queries each system in place, so no data is migrated, and access follows the identity and permission controls the agency already has.
  3. Skills and connectors come together in agents, including pre-built agents from public sector software providers that agencies can deploy right away. They handle tasks like FOIA discovery and batch redaction under the same central governance, with a person approving each consequential step.
  4. A governed control plane: Security and compliance teams get one place to set and enforce policy across every agent, including VPC Service Controls, CMEK, and Assured Workloads. Outputs are grounded in source documents, with citations, so reviewers can check where each answer came from.
  5. An open partner ecosystem: Every agency works under a different statute and runs a different mix of systems. System integrators and public sector ISVs help agencies customize Gemini, connect it to what they already have, and scale it without lock-in.

Skills for government workflows

Gemini for government services helps automate and accelerate complex government operations, including:

  • Policy and regulatory research: Ask an operational or eligibility question and get an answer drawn from the CFR, the Federal Register, state administrative codes, and internal manuals, with page and paragraph citations. Where federal and state rules both apply, Gemini shows which one governs to empower agency decision makers.
  • : Gemini searches SharePoint, Drive, and email archives for records responsive to a FOIA or state Sunshine Law request. It organizes them into a review set for the records officer and agency counsel, shortening discovery that often takes weeks.
  • Redaction for public release: Gemini finds sensitive constituent data across a batch of documents, groups the findings so reviewers can clear them in passes, and proposes redactions labeled by statutory exemption. After a reviewer confirms, it produces the exemption log and audit-ready copies.
  • : Gemini checks multi-volume bids against RFP requirements, FAR guidelines, minimum mandatory criteria, and evaluation rubrics, and returns scoring justifications with citations. Contracting officers get a documented basis for each award decision.
  • Grant and program expense audits: Gemini checks invoices, receipts, purchase orders, and ledger entries against 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance and the terms of the award. It flags unallowable costs, missing documentation, and funding discrepancies with line-item citations, so problems surface while there's still time to fix them.
  • Document validation at intake: Gemini classifies and validates pay stubs, W-2s, utility bills, and leases when they arrive, checks the numbers for consistency, and flags missing signatures. Defects are caught before the application enters the queue, not weeks into the case.
  • : Gemini turns policy memos and agency guidance into public notices, aligned to the Plain Writing Act of 2010, USDA-FNS standards, and Title VI language access guidance.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the government technology stack

Gemini for government services connects directly to core agency systems via secure connectors. Access is bound by existing role-based access controls, record-level permissions, and the trusted data controls inherited from each system — and nothing is migrated to make the connection work.

Federal regulatory and public data:

  • Tracks legislative actions, regulations, and executive orders as they post, so state and local teams see federal changes as they land.
  • Tracks federal rulemaking dockets, public comments, and statutory agency response deadlines, keeping policy analysts ahead of incoming mandates.
  • eCFR (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations): Grounds answers in the governing regulation, with citations down to the paragraph.

Agency systems of record:

  • Gives agents permission-bound access to procurement, payables, and ledger transactions for expense auditing and award reconciliation.
  • Connects HR and personnel records under existing role-based controls, so workforce questions are answered from the system of record.
  • Enables conversational experiences across the Missionforce portfolio through headless integration with Gemini, including benefits, licensing, permitting, and contact center management.
  • Automates IT, CRM, security, employee experience, and workflow records, so agents can track incidents, requests, and approval chains inside existing routing rules.

Productivity and collaboration:

  • Connects with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to analyze case communications and agency correspondence and surface internal files while enforcing agency access controls.
  • Microsoft 365 and SharePoint: Integrates with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint to triage inquiries and ground responses in mail and intranet repositories without breaking workflow context.

Third-party agents and implementation partners

Every agency operates differently. Through our open platform, agencies can deploy pre-built partner agents or work with system integrators to scale custom capabilities:

  • SZNS Solutions FOIA and public records discovery agent: Turns a plain-language request, a piece of correspondence, or a formal citizen inquiry into a scoped search across enterprise archives — bounded by custodian and date range, so a records officer narrows the set before any data moves. It exports responsive material into secure agency repositories and tracks delivery status, giving each request an auditable trail from intake to release.
  • SZNS Solutions document redaction agent: Works inside connected repositories — SharePoint and Drive among them — finding sensitive citizen data across a batch and grouping the findings so a reviewer clears them in passes rather than page by page. Each proposed redaction carries its statutory exemption, and once the reviewer confirms, the agent exports permanently redacted, audit-ready copies back to the system of record, with the processing never leaving the agency's cloud perimeter.
  • Systems integrators & tech partners: Strategic partnerships with Accenture Federal Services, Clutch, Dark Wolf, Daston, Deloitte, Egen, Game Plan Tech, Knexus, Onix, Resultant, SAIC, Slalom, and SZNS Solutions so agencies can customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside federal, state, and local government agencies

We are working closely with select federal and state agencies, including the State of Missouri and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to ensure these capabilities work in day-to-day agency operations.

"Our citizens expect the government to move at the speed of modern life, not the speed of paperwork. By automating routine work in our workflows, we're delivering faster, better services to Missourians." - Tim Marczewski, Director of AI and Innovation, State of Missouri Office of Administration.

Built on an enterprise-grade foundation

Gemini for government services runs on Google Cloud's secure foundation, and can be deployed using the Assured Workloads FedRAMP High Data Boundary, enforcing U.S. data residency and personnel controls. It works within the authorities, retention rules, and approval chains your agency already has.

Agency records, constituent data, institutional documents, custom agents, and model outputs stay private to your organization, and are never used to train or fine-tune Google's foundation models without your permission. Because we operate the full stack, from infrastructure and models through the application layer, we can tune performance and cost together — routing high-volume document parsing and routine records sweeps to fast, low-cost models and reserving high-reasoning models for complex policy analysis, so expanding what your teams can take on does not mean expanding spend at the same rate.

This is just the beginning

The launch of Gemini for government services represents another defining step in delivering on our promise to bring the best of Gemini to every professional, for every workflow, natively tailored to the way they work.

Gemini for government services is available in today, joining our purpose-built solutions for industries. We invite leaders at every level of government to explore how Gemini can transform their most critical workflows.

items.title: Enabling the next era of sovereign AI: The latest Google Distributed Cloud innovations
items.author: Muninder SambiVP, Product Management & Supply Chain, Google Distributed Cloud
items.content:
Agentic systems are quickly moving from pilots to production in the enterprise. But if your organization operates under stringent data sovereignty, defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure mandates, sending sensitive data to a public cloud often isn’t an option — and building your own AI stack inside a disconnected perimeter can take months. Your missions demand frontier models, hardened security, and high performance, deployed directly where your most sensitive data lives.

The latest innovations in Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped represent a huge leap forward for organizations struggling with these challenges, and they no longer need to make this tradeoff. Enterprise search capabilities with Gemini, support for open weight models, turnkey ISV applications, next-generation accelerated infrastructure, and support for new partners are all now available to be directly deployed in your sovereign, air-gapped environments.

Here’s a high-level look at the major capabilities launching across three pillars: Sovereign AI and enterprise search, next-generation infrastructure, and a growing ISV partner ecosystem.

GDC technology stack: Infra, frontier models, data and applications

The GDC technology stack turns isolated infrastructure into a modern agentic innovation platform, combining foundational and open model flexibility, intuitive out-of-the-box user experiences, and high-performance data processing.

We are excited to bring the following innovations to GDC:

  • Gemini on GDC enterprise search: In air-gapped environments, analysts and knowledge workers spend critical hours manually sifting through compartmentalized documents, intercepted audio, and sensor video. Agentic systems can streamline those processes, but building those capabilities often requires months of custom development. With enterprise search capabilities in Gemini on GDC (available in preview), organizations gain a turnkey conversational interface, so they can query, prompt, and summarize vast repositories of data near-instantaneously. Unlike text-only open-source alternatives, this managed architecture delivers native multi-modality support via Gemini embedding models, combining high-throughput scaling and low-latency inference performance for text, audio, and video modalities. Built-in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) keeps indexing and interactions strictly within your sovereign perimeter, accelerating insights without compromising security.
  • Expanded frontier and open-weight models: Google Cloud is one of the first hyperscalers to bring a frontier model like Gemini to air-gapped deployments. Now generally available on GDC air-gapped, delivers ultra-low-latency reasoning, multimodal understanding, and long-context capabilities entirely within your air-gapped boundary, allowing users to process large volumes of field intelligence, from reports to imagery and recordings, quickly. GDC also now supports leading open models like and , giving you architectural and workload choice, giving you the flexibility to match the right model to each workload on the same governed platform.

Next-generation IaaS powering GDC

To run modern agentic systems and memory-intensive enterprise workloads on the same infrastructure, you need an uncompromising foundation. GDC air-gapped features a new, elevated Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) stack across compute, networking, and security, so you can run AI and traditional workloads side by side with the performance and protection they need.

  • Next-gen high-performance agentic infrastructure:NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture are now generally available on GDC air-gapped, giving you the local compute to serve Gemini and open models — and the agents built on them — at production scale. Paired with VM networking that now supports up to 32 Gbps per VM (up from 25 Gbps), you can move data to your GPUs faster and reduce bottlenecks in your inference pipelines.
  • Resilient, enterprise-grade networking: Fully managed Cloud DNS, now generally available on GDC, lets your platform teams manage DNS records with the same Kubernetes APIs and command line they already use — with no third-party DNS infrastructure to deploy, patch, and maintain inside the air gap. And hardware-offloaded IPsec encryption protects node-to-node traffic at up to 100 Gbps, helping you meet encryption-in-transit requirements without taking CPU away from your applications.
  • SecOps enabled by Elastic: As agentic workloads scale, you need machine-speed security to defend your distributed environments. Through our deep integration with , we are modernizing threat detection and response (SIEM and EDR) on GDC air-gapped. Together, Elastic Security and GDC air-gapped provide automated case management, behavioral analytics, and agentic-driven telemetry correlation, so you can accelerate your mean time to response (MTTR).

Expanding the sovereign ISV partner ecosystem

Your missions depend on more than infrastructure — they run on the data platforms, developer tools, and collaboration apps your teams already know. That’s why we’re bringing more of that software to run natively on GDC, so you can adopt AI without leaving familiar tools behind. Today, we’re expanding the GDC partner marketplace with independent software vendors (ISVs) including Teradata, Solo.io, and Mattermost:

  • extends industry-standard enterprise data analytics and warehouse intelligence to the distributed edge, so you can run complex analytical pipelines right next to local AI inference — and act on insights without moving data outside your perimeter.
  • brings API management, service mesh, and agentic networking — including kagent and agentgateway — to sovereign deployments, so you can securely connect and govern microservices and AI agents across isolated clusters, including which tools and other agents each agent can reach.
  • delivers secure collaboration and mission-critical operations workflows for defense and public sector teams, so your people can coordinate in real time entirely inside the air gap — including AI-assisted summaries and translation using models running locally on GDC.

Building the future of sovereign cloud

With these capabilities, sovereignty no longer has to slow down your AI ambitions. By bringing Gemini and open-weight models, multimodal enterprise search, high-performance infrastructure, built-in security, and a growing ISV ecosystem together inside your air-gapped perimeter, GDC helps you turn your most sensitive data into actionable insights, while you maintain compliance, security, and control.

items.title: Announcements and highlights from Google Public Sector Summit 2026
items.author: Karen DahutCEO, Google Public Sector
items.content:
Today we are bringing together mission leaders and builders from across the public sector at the Google Public Sector Summit in Washington D.C. to explore a critical intersection: Where mission meets moonshot. Through our hands-on programming, we will offer inspiration as well as pragmatic steps for turning moonshot aspirations into secure, scaled, real-world outcomes.

From mapping the human genome to putting a human on the moon, public sector organizations have been at the helm of some of humanity’s most historic breakthroughs. Right now, public sector leaders are being asked to move faster than ever, amidst more complexity and uncertainty, often with fewer resources than the mission demands. To better understand these challenges and opportunities, we surveyed several hundred leaders from across the public sector with theCUBE and ECI Research. According to the findings, while of agencies have deployed agents in some form, only have achieved agency-wide adoption. The bottleneck isn’t a lack of vision or ambition—it is the systemic friction of legacy data silos and integration complexity. That is why so many organizations turn to Google; we deliver powerful technology that reduces the toil of getting started, minimizes the friction of integration, and provides the secure foundation for scale.

To that end, we are excited to share several new announcements and capabilities to support your missions and moonshots in the agentic era.

Introducing the Gemini agent

We recently announced the Gemini agent: your new single, universal agent for work. It can have all of your organizational context and can be used for everything from knowledge work to answering questions, and from content creation to coding, all from a single prompt box. At your direction, it can plan the work, use skills and tools, connect to your systems, and bring back something finished — inside the documents, the inbox, and the developer environments you already work in and give it permissions for. With your guidance, the agent chooses the best model for the job, employs built-in cost controls, and most importantly, reflects the security, administration, and governance controls established by your organization.

Introducing Gemini for government services

This morning we launched Gemini for government services in private preview, a purpose-built platform engineered for the security, governance, and workflow complexity of public sector missions. Built around the core promise of delivering "less paperwork, more public service," it provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies. By combining pre-built partner agents, secure connectors, and deterministic skills, the platform enables civil servants to securely link Gemini directly to existing case management, ERP, and agency collaboration systems of record without migrating their agencies’ sensitive data. Civil servants are empowered to automate repetitive, high-stakes tasks—such as public records requests, document intake validation, expense auditing, and policy research—all grounded in authoritative federal regulatory sources with verifiable citations. Learn more about Gemini for government services in our blog post.

Introducing Wiz agents in Wiz for Gov

The Wiz Red, Green, and Blue agents are now available within Wiz for Gov, Wiz’s FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment. The expansion of the agent trio into Wiz for Gov accelerates remediation for critical public sector priorities, including Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The Green Agent can assist in driving PQC readiness through a new risk type dedicated to weak cryptography that investigates whether an asset is quantum-vulnerable and assesses potential Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) exposure. By leveraging the cryptographic visibility from code to runtime gained through the Wiz AI-APP, the Wiz Green Agent is able to help weigh real-world external reachability against data sensitivity enabling delivery of continuously updated, PQC-resistant fixes directly into developer workflows.

Wiz has also invested in several other initiatives intended to benefit the public sector. Scan for Good, a program launched jointly by Wiz and Google DeepMind, uses the Wiz Red Agent and Gemini 4 Argon, alongside Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, to provide no-cost security assessments designed to uncover high-risk vulnerabilities and exposures across eligible public services, critical infrastructure, and other under-resourced organizations. Wiz is also expanding capabilities for organizations navigating the new FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rulesets. This includes operationalizing critical FedRAMP metrics, including Potential Agency Impact (PAIN), and validating likely exploitability (LEV) and internet reachability (IRV). These enhancements will assist organizations seeking to achieve or maintain FedRAMP certification with the automated reporting and prioritized risk assessment required.

Bringing enterprise search capabilities to Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud

For defense, intelligence, and national security agencies operating in classified environments, the challenge is not just analyzing vast volumes of sensitive data, it is doing so without compromising perimeter security. To help turn classified information into actionable intelligence, we are bringing enterprise search capabilities to Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud for air-gapped deployments. With this new capability, users gain an intuitive conversational interface to query, synthesize, and summarize records at machine speed, completely disconnected from the public internet. This launch brings Gemini 3.5 Flash models to on-premises air-gapped deployments, expands model flexibility with open models like Gemma, and delivers massive local compute through generally available NVIDIA Blackwell B300 GPUs.

Driving mission impact, together

Through partnership and powerful technology, organizations across the public sector are transforming how services are delivered, accelerating research and science, strengthening national security, improving healthcare delivery, and enhancing student outcomes. These organizations aren’t waiting for the future; they are actively building it right now.

  • is offering a streamlined "front door" that simplifies access to federal services online. Google is proud to be named a technology partner in this vital initiative, leveraging Gemini to help millions of Americans access critical public resources with greater speed and ease.
  • is tackling challenges with direct impact for communities across New York and beyond. Together, we are ​​empowering researchers of all technical backgrounds to easily access and benefit from Google Cloud's advanced capabilities—bringing storage, high-powered computing, Gemini Enterprise, and more than 200 trusted models together into a seamless, centralized ecosystem.
  • is accelerating breakthroughs in energy dominance, discovery science, and national security through the Genesis Mission. Gemini will support the full breadth of work - from the research bench to specialized user facilities – building a secure foundation that the DOE mission can depend on.
  • is leading a sweeping modernization of its logistics infrastructure including non-tactical logistics networks, supply chain procedures, and organic industrial base sites. The Army's Strategic Capital Initiative will pair Google's secure cloud and FedEx's logistics expertise to build a more intelligent and connected supply chain network that helps reduce delivery times and ensures personnel receive the critical equipment where and when they need it.
  • is supercharging daily operations and workflows with Gemini, giving 3 million personnel across the department access to a secure enterprise-grade platform. With Agent Designer, GenAI.mil users are quickly able to build their own agents using natural language to help streamline repetitive, multi-step tasks such as document creation and document reviews.
  • Case Western Reserve University is improving learning outcomes and accelerating research breakthroughs. They are leveraging Gemini for education campus-wide, transforming the experience of every scientist, staff member, and student. Tomorrow, they’re opening a new hub for discovery and innovation that leverages Google technology, and connects Google engineers with 300 university researchers across campus.

Google Public Sector: Your mission partner

The agentic era will not be defined by what technology can do, but by what we choose to build with it. So let’s meet this moment, let's re-imagine what’s possible, and let’s create impact — together.
